PART II · CHAPTER 6

## Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

One adapter family over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA interfaces carries every record into the event backbone, so no source system is ever loaded, modified or replaced, and no join is trusted until it is proven on a real week of production data.

Chapter 5 showed what the object model holds and how one walk crosses its links. This chapter covers how records reach it: through one adapter family, never directly, and never with a join trusted before it is proven.

### 6.1  Eight Sources, One Door Each

Eight sources feed the design. Five are named systems of record, all of the operator's own and all read only: the manufacturing execution system, the system of record for lots, routes, recipes, tool states and holds, where every trace ends in a lot and a hold; the yield management system, which holds wafer maps, signatures and excursion records; the inspection tools' own defect databases, the source of defect candidates and review images the edge units classify; the equipment data collection system, which carries chamber sensor telemetry and FDC traces for drift precursors and excursion tracing; and the statistical process control system, which holds the control limits a wafer map signature crossing triggers on. The remaining sources are the tool interfaces and telemetry streams at the edge. Figure 5 maps each named system, its provenance class and its adapter path into the backbone.

![Figure 5. The 8 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.](figures/figure_05.png)

Figure 5. The 8 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

### 6.2  What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One adapter family, the integration adapter, carries every record in, over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA interfaces decided by which revisions each etch module tool implements. The tier guarantees four things. First, no source is ever loaded, modified or replaced: the adapters read, and nothing is written back toward a system of record except an approved hold or disposition through the manufacturing execution system interface. Second, every record carries its provenance and its timestamp, so any figure on any surface can be traced to the system that holds its truth. Third, event logs are constructed in the pipeline layer rather than trusted as they arrive, because source systems differ in what they call an event and when they record it. Fourth, no join is trusted until it is proven: the adapters reconcile the source keys across the systems on one real week of production data before phase one is judged, recording where the truth actually lives, because an ontology that joins silently wrong keys is worse than four systems that do not join at all.

### 6.3  The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka with KRaft, and it answers four questions. Ordering: events are keyed per wafer and per tool, so inspection runs, defect candidates and telemetry replay in the sequence they happened. Delivery: adapters are at least once and idempotent, so a replayed event cannot double count a defect or a confirmed class. Buffering: the backbone absorbs bursts when a review tool emits images faster than the edge tier classifies them, and the edge units buffer locally when their uplink is briefly lost. Replication: topics are replicated across brokers so the loss of a broker does not lose records, and the artifact registry in Harbor keeps the edge tier's software resynchronizable without any internet path. Time alignment across sensors and systems is held by Linuxptp against an Open Time Card grandmaster class clock, so an FDC trace, an inspection run and a wafer map signature from the same excursion share one clock. Nothing on the backbone crosses the fab perimeter.

PART II · CHAPTER 7

## Classification Runs at the Tool, Reasoning Inside

The anomaly classifier runs on sealed fanless units at the inspection tools with no internet path, while reasoning waits on verified open weights self hosted inside the fab, and the latency budget is set by images arriving, not by users waiting.

Chapter 6 followed every record from the fab's systems of record through the adapter tier into the object model. This chapter follows the same data one step further, to where it is computed: which model runs on a sealed unit at the inspection tool, which runs on the operator's own servers deeper inside the fab, and what that split costs in latency and failure exposure.

### 7.1  Two Tiers, Each Placed for a Reason

The design has two inference tiers, and Figure 6 sets them side by side with what runs on each and what crosses between them. The first tier is the tool itself. Sealed fanless units beside the optical inspection and electron microscope review tools classify defect images as they arrive, on the CodeNinja on-device AI stack runtime, using an unsupervised anomaly model fitted on this fab's own normal images, so a class candidate exists before any image leaves the tool bay. The unit is an octa core edge SoC class with a 6 TOPS neural processing unit, commercial grade rated 0 to 80 C, in a fanless sealed smooth-wall cleanroom enclosure with a power over Ethernet front end, because a fan sheds and moves particles. The arithmetic that matters at this tier is load, not weights: the NPU load figures on the on-device shelf were measured for detectors rather than an anomaly model, so a 60 percent headroom gate governs until the real load is measured, and a saturated unit dropping images silently is the named failure mode behind that gate.

The second tier is inside the fab, on the operator's own servers. The stack row that names GLM 5.3 calls it a 753-billion-parameter model at FP8 precision and node class, which is exactly why no language model is served at the tool. What the plan holds for this tier is the class and the rule: a 141 GB high bandwidth memory GPU class with 8 GPUs per node, and the frontier model footprint sizing rule for vLLM and SGLang serving. What it does not hold is the split between weights, usable memory and the KV cache ceiling, because no verified model row stands in the register; those figures are derived only when one does, and Chapter 8 explains why none does yet.

![Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.](figures/figure_06.png)

Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

### 7.2  Latency Runs From Image Arrival to Hold Approval

The budget has two ends, and neither is a person waiting on a chat reply. At the near end, classification sits in the arrival path: the unit must keep pace with the inspection tool's own output, and the headroom gate exists so that bursts of arrivals never queue behind a saturated unit. At the far end sits the rollout's own measure, time from excursion onset to hold, with a nominal of 4.0 hours and a breach above it, exercised by the simulated event of one etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer maps. Everything between, from the wafer map signature crossing a control limit, through the excursion agent tracing it to a chamber, to the yield engineer approving the hold, must fit inside that figure. The people in the loop pace the budget and guard it at once, and that is deliberate: how inspection AI is classified is an active regulatory question, with published analyzes of risk classification and compliance pathways for AI-based visual quality inspection (KB 2025), so every class candidate and every hold draft ends with a named approver rather than acting alone.

### 7.3  What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails When It Does

Nothing crosses the fab perimeter. Tool-to-server flows ride internal segmented conduits under the fab's own cybersecurity program, no edge unit gets any internet path, and the event backbone, Apache Kafka in KRaft mode, carries class candidates, defect records, wafer map signatures and heartbeats between the tiers, with linuxptp and an Open Time Card grandmaster class keeping event order honest across systems. Each failure mode is bounded. If the link fails, classification continues at the tool because the classifier is local, and queued events move when the conduit returns, while the surfaces show the gap honestly. If power fails, the unit drops with it, since power arrives on the same Ethernet front end, and the edge unit heartbeat puts the drop on the health surface where someone sees it. If the update path fails, nothing is pushed from outside, because there is no outside path: artifacts and model updates move through Harbor, the air-gapped artifact and model registry, on the internal network, and a unit that misses an update keeps running its last verified artifact until the path returns.

PART II · CHAPTER 8

## No Weights Are Committed Before Verification

The register is honestly empty: no open weight model survived this run's live checks, so GLM 5.3 stands as a named intention with an unsized footprint rather than a committed row, and the gate to commit it is verification, not preference.

Chapter 7 placed classification at the tool and reasoning inside the fab, and it left one number deliberately unfixed: the size of the reasoning footprint. This chapter shows why the register is empty, what stands in it instead, and what it will take to commit a model row.

![Figure 7. The two models, their placement, and the work each one does.](figures/figure_07.png)

Figure 7. The two models, their placement, and the work each one does.

### 8.1  An Honest Register Holds One Intention and One Fitted Model

Figure 7 lays the model stack out, and its most important feature is an absence: the register holds no model row, because no open weight model survived this run's live checks. The catalog entries the tooling lens brought in were each verified by a person on the date the entry carries and were not rechecked live for this build, and that outstanding verification is the gate to commit, not a matter of preference. GLM 5.3 therefore stands as a named intention. The operator's own ask names it, reasoning on GLM 5.3 open weights, self hosted inside the fab, acquired by a commercial buyer, and the work surface commits frontier-class open weights self hosted for sovereignty, of GLM 5.3 or Kimi class. Behind the name stand a role and a placement: reasoning for the three named agents and for the command center's conversational interface that answers with citations, running on the operator's own servers inside the fab, never at the tool, never as a third party model service. Behind it do not stand a filed parameter count, precision, license terms or context window, so the footprint is unsized and no GPU count is derived; the stack row that calls GLM 5.3 a 753-billion-parameter FP8 node-class model is the argument for where it sits, not a committed figure. Committing the row means a live check on this build, filed together with the parameter count, precision and license terms, and only then does the sizing rule fix the node count, the weights against usable memory and the KV cache ceiling.

The second model in the stack is not a language model at all. The edge tier runs an unsupervised anomaly model fitted on this fab's own normal images, served on the CodeNinja on-device AI stack runtime at the tool. It was chosen against a defect classifier trained on labelled images, for two reasons the design states plainly: System of context forbids a model trained for this operator, and a trained-classifier estate becomes a standing retraining burden. Confirmed classes and root causes become memory instead, and no weight is ever updated by them. Assurance cannot lean on mature certification here, because the functional safety and AI standard is a technical report (ISO 2024), so the design's own gates carry it: the phase one bench run measures the anomaly model on the fab's own images, and no accuracy is quotable before that run.

An empty register is not a gap in the design; it is the design holding its own rule. The operator is buying weights it will hold, so which weights is part of what is being bought, and a row that could not survive a live check would be a costly line in the build.

### 8.2  The Choice Register on One Page

Table 4 gathers what the register does hold: each model with its status, the hardware classes and the sizing rule, the sensing the design stands on, the pattern, and the ground it runs on. Read as a whole, it says that everything is committed except the weights themselves, and that the weights wait on verification rather than preference.

Table 4 · Model and Equipment Register

| The choice | What was picked | Why here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reasoning model | GLM 5.3, open weights, self hosted inside the fab, acquired by a commercial buyer | Named in the operator's own ask; sovereignty requires weights the operator holds; unsized until the row survives a live check |
| Edge classifier | Unsupervised anomaly model fitted on the fab's own normal images, served on the CodeNinja on-device AI stack runtime at the tool | System of context forbids a model trained for this operator; a trained classifier would be a standing retraining burden; confirmed classes become memory |
| Edge hardware class | Octa core 6 TOPS NPU edge SoC class, commercial grade 0 to 80 C, fanless sealed smooth-wall cleanroom enclosure, PoE front end | No fan sheds or moves particles; shelf figures are measured for detectors, so the 60 percent headroom gate governs until the anomaly load is measured |
| Site hardware class | 141 GB HBM GPU class, 8 GPUs per node, on the operator's own hardware inside the fab | Frontier-class open weights at FP8 are node class; no GPU count is derived while no verified model row stands |
| Sizing rule | Frontier model footprint sizing rule for vLLM and SGLang serving | Fixes the node count, weights against usable memory and the KV cache ceiling |

PART III · CHAPTER 9

## One Etch Module Quarter Proves It First

Phase one is one etch module for one quarter, gated on classification quality on this fab's own images, joins proven on production data and named approvals on every hold, before any extension gate opens.

Chapter 8 ended with the register's honest gap: the weights the operator named sit in the catalog, but no model survived this run's live checks, so the fab's inference server stays unsized until a verified model stands in the register. This chapter turns that honesty into sequence: the riskiest assumption, classification quality on this fab's own images, is proven first on one etch module, and every extension gate opens only on recorded evidence.

### 9.1  Phases, Gates and Coverage

Phase One is the etch module phase: 17 items across six workstreams, namely approvals and security, the command center, memory, the named agents with engineers deciding, one model of the fab, and the phase one gates. The items include the units placed at the inspection tools, the hardening of the zero shot defect classifier, and the fab ontology of yield objects, the 16 objects from wafer to process owner. Its exit gate is zero shot defect classifier hardening: the anomaly model is measured offline on a development board against this fab's own images before any accuracy figure is quoted, and only ranges with stated conditions are quotable before that bench run. Phase Two carries a single item, the extension gates and module rollout, and it opens only when Phase One's gates have been judged against recorded baselines. Figure 8 sets both phases, their item counts and their gates side by side, with requirement coverage beside them: the plan's coverage record holds the requirement covered, with nothing partial and nothing open.

![Figure 8. The two phases and their gates, and coverage of the one requirement across them.](figures/figure_08.png)

Figure 8. The two phases and their gates, and coverage of the one requirement across them.

### 9.2  What the Rollout Measures

The loop is judged on one measure: time from excursion onset to hold, in hours, with a nominal of 4.0 and a breach when the measured time rises above it. The fault that exercises the measure is the design's simulated event, one etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer maps. The excursion agent must trace that signature to a chamber through the equipment data collection traces, draft a hold, and a yield engineer must approve it before the clock stops. Baselines and counting rules are agreed before the first model is fitted, a discipline the sector's own precedents taught, and since neither precedent published a false-call rate, the nuisance trend surface carries ranges with conditions rather than a single figure. Machine learning already runs across nearly every safety-critical industry, which is why these gates are agreed in advance and judged against recorded baselines rather than after the fact (Nationalacademies 2025), and the hold refusal rule is anchored in code in the spirit of functional safety guidance for AI systems (ISO 2024).

### 9.3  Failure Modes

Table 5 states what can fail and what the design does about each failure, and every mitigation named in it is an item or a gate already carried by a phase.

Table 5 · Failure Modes

| What fails | What the design does |
| --- | --- |
| Anomaly model quality on this fab's images is unmeasured until the bench run | Dev board and offline measurement on the fab's own images is the phase gate; only ranges with conditions are quoted before it |
| NPU load figures are measured for detectors, not the anomaly model, and a saturated unit drops images silently | Commit the stronger SoC class, measure the actual load, and keep the 60 percent headroom gate |
| Deemed export of fab technology if a supporting engineer is a non-US person | Screen the support team under the EAR deemed export rule before access is granted, and name the check as an approval |
| A hold placed or released without a recorded named approval | The approval-missing attempt is refused in code and audited per hold; the gate is the MES interface, never the agent |
| Ontology joins fail silently when source keys do not reconcile across the systems | Prove the joins on one real week of production data before Phase One is judged, and record where the truth actually lives |
| A managed cloud or third-party model service appearing anywhere in the build | Confirm the sovereign obligation with the operator's compliance owner and bind it to a named scope item before design freeze |

### 9.4  Lessons

**Agree the baselines and counting rules before the first model ships.** The sector's precedent builds that skipped this step spent their first measured period arguing about what counted as a defect rather than improving the model; this plan fixes the counting rules as a gate item, so the bench run measures against a settled definition and the false-call question is asked with the same denominators throughout. Design drift handling in from version one. The simulated event is a chamber drifting gradually and printing a ring signature, not a step change, so the excursion path, the chamber telemetry precursors and the hold drafting are exercised from the first version rather than retrofitted after a first excursion is missed. Fit the classifier on this fab's own images. The pattern the history lens surfaced is that an image model learns the fab, not the defect: a model fitted elsewhere inherits another fab's illumination, another tool's artifacts and another process's nuisance population. The anomaly model is therefore fitted unsupervised on this fab's own normal images, and no edge unit holds any internet path.

### 9.5  What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open, and each settles into a design change. The false-call rate: neither sector precedent published one, and settling it would let the nuisance trend surface carry a single quotable figure instead of ranges with conditions. The model register: no open-weight model survived this run's live checks, so the reasoning weights the operator named are not yet sized under the register; settling it fixes the fab's inference server, its GPU count under the 141 GB HBM rule and its license terms. The sovereign obligation: the rule of no cloud and no third party model service is confirmed with the operator's own compliance owner and bound to a named scope item before design freeze, and settling it removes the last condition on the boundary the ownership chapter describes.

PART III · CHAPTER 10

## The Intelligence Stays with the Fab Producing It

The ontology, the memory of confirmed classes and root causes, the decision record and the boundary all belong to the operator, held on its own hardware, and the agents never place or release a hold without a named approval.

Chapter 9 set the gates that protect the build's integrity; this chapter states who holds what those gates protect, which is the operator, on every axis that matters.

### 10.1  Who Owns What the Build Produces

The operator owns the object model. The 16 objects and their typed links are a projection over the operator's own systems of record, never a shadow copy of them, and the crossing mappings that answer questions no single system can are held with the ontology. Unlike most industrial ontology examples, which live in a vendor's documentation, this one lives on the operator's own hardware and changes only through its named owners. The operator owns the memory: every confirmed class and every confirmed root cause is kept as decision memory that the next run reads before it acts, and because nothing is trained or distilled into weights under system of context, there are no fine-tunes whose ownership could ever be contested; the anomaly model is fitted unsupervised on the fab's own normal images and runs where the fab runs. The operator owns the decision record: every hold carries who raised it and who approved it, the approval-missing attempt is refused in code, and the audit trail per hold is the operator's own evidence, produced by its own people acting under its own authority. The operator owns the boundary: the whole build runs on the operator's own hardware inside the fab, nothing crosses the fab perimeter, no managed cloud service and no third-party model service appears anywhere, and the support team is screened under the EAR deemed export rule before any access is granted.

### 10.2  The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and the design maps directly onto what CodeNinja builds: the governed object model of wafers, lots, tools, chambers, excursions and holds is Hyper Ontology; the command center where the yield team works excursions, holds, tool risk and agent drafts, and where the operator's own people can build further agents on models they can change without losing what was built, is Hyper Pragma; the three named agents that draft classifications, excursion traces and dispositions for a named engineer to confirm and approve are Decision Systems; and the whole posture, open weights on hardware the operator owns inside its own fab with no third-party model service, is Sovereign Infrastructure.

PART IV · CONCLUSION

## The Fab Should Reason Over Its Own Records

One design holds the whole argument: classification at the tool on sealed fanless units, one governed ontology joining eight sources into sixteen objects, three named agents that draft while named engineers decide, memory of confirmed classes and root causes instead of retraining, and every byte staying inside the fab boundary on hardware the operator owns, with the model register stating plainly that no weights are committed until a verified row stands.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes an operation willing to name its systems of record and its approvers before the first model is discussed, edge units rated for the floor environment rather than adapted office hardware, an export control screen on every supporting engineer before access is granted, and a first phase aimed at the riskiest assumption, classification quality on that fab's own images, rather than the widest scope.

PART IV · CHAPTER 11

## How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice in this design traces to recorded reading: eight reasoning lenses and the brief in the operator's own words.

Chapter 10 closed the argument on ownership; this chapter opens the record, so a reader can trace any choice in the paper back to the reading that justified it. Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for designing physical AI systems, and Figure 9 shows the path from the ask to the reasoning to the design.

### 11.1  Contextualizing the Ask

The ask, in the operator's own words, was a physical AI system for wafer defect inspection and yield analytics: edge units next to optical inspection and electron microscope review tools classifying defect images as they arrive, one governed fab ontology joining the manufacturing execution, yield management, tool defect, equipment data collection and statistical process control systems, three named agents drafting for engineers who confirm and approve, memory keeping every confirmed class and root cause, reasoning self hosted inside the fab, and one simulated event, an etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer maps. Praxis assigned the design to the Enterprise AI family; the semiconductors pin is the FDE's own decision on this project, stated as a decision rather than a reasoned match, and the brief was read as reasoning input.

### 11.2  The Lenses

Table 6 states what each of the eight lenses could see, how many sources it cited and what it contributed to the design. Every lens returned a contribution; the gap in this design is not a lens that saw nothing but a register that could not yet stand behind weights, which the tooling lens records plainly.

### 11.3  Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

System of context was adopted as the primary pattern, pinned by the FDE, because the requirement asks exactly for its shape: a governed ontology tied to source systems that are never replaced, never modified and never loaded, agents that draft while engineers decide, and memory that improves without training. Its fixed grammar governs the whole build: nouns become objects, facts become properties, relationships become typed links, and actions change them. No pattern was set aside; the reasoning trace records none, and the design carries no orphaned architecture.

### 11.4  Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on equipment classes rather than named products wherever the shelf holds no verified entry: the octa-core 6 TOPS NPU edge SoC class in fanless sealed cleanroom enclosures, the Open Time Card grandmaster class for time synchronization, the 141 GB HBM GPU class for the fab's inference server, and fab integration decided tool by tool over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA according to which revisions each etch-module tool implements. Two precedents were read in the sector, the Seagate fab image defect build and the SK hynix virtual metrology build, and both shaped the phase gates rather than decorating the prose. Everything shown in this chapter was recorded reading: the citation counts and the gap in the model register are as recorded, and nothing is inferred.

Appendix A

## What the Fab's Own Reasoning Node Costs Over Three Years

The paper is written for a high volume wafer fab in the United States, with an on-site server room on the fab's segmented tool network where the reasoning model runs on the operator's own hardware (chapter 1, section 1.3). This appendix therefore prices for the United States, with the national average industrial and commercial electricity prices for power and the AWS US East (N. Virginia) region, us-east-1, as the rental reference. The design runs every model on hardware the operator owns, and its site tier is GLM 5.3 at FP8, which "need[s] a full node of the 141 GB HBM GPU class, eight GPUs per node, to themselves" (chapter 3, section 3.1; Table 4, "Site hardware class"; Figure 9, "the 141 GB HBM sizing table fixed the GLM 5.3 node count at one"). Chapter 8 keeps that footprint formally unsized until a verified register row stands, so this appendix prices the one node chapter 3 and Figure 9 name, and nothing beyond it. The edge tier needs no line here: the paper names the class of the edge unit (an octa core 6 TOPS NPU SoC in a fanless sealed cleanroom enclosure, Table 4) and places one per inspection tool group (Table 2), but gives neither a unit price nor a count of tool groups, so nothing is added for it rather than a count guessed. The node is priced two ways: owned, from a reseller's published configured price with support and power added, and rented, from the AWS price files for us-east-1, on demand and on the two three year all upfront plans. Every input is dated and cited, and the arithmetic is shown.

### A.1 The Answer

Owning the node for three years costs **about 576,000 US dollars**, inside a range of 551,000 to 623,000. Renting the same eight H200 cards around the clock costs **about 625,000 dollars** on the deepest three year commitment (an AWS EC2 Instance Savings Plan, all upfront, for p5en.48xlarge in US East (N. Virginia)), **about 1.11 million dollars** on the three year Compute Savings Plan, all upfront, and **about 1.66 million dollars** on demand. Against the deepest commitment, ownership costs **about nine tenths** (575,786 / 625,446 = 0.92, and 0.88 to 1.00 across the range); against on demand, about a third (575,786 / 1,663,419 = 0.35). Renting is a price reference only: every rented option would carry process data and wafer images out of the fab to a third party, which the operator's own constraint of open weights on hardware it owns, with no third party model service and nothing crossing the fab perimeter, rules out (chapter 3, section 3.1; Table 2, "Model serving"; chapter 10). The paper files no license terms for GLM 5.3 (chapter 8, section 8.1), so no license line is asserted here.

The power line is a ceiling: it takes the configurator's maximum estimate around the clock, and a reasoning node serving three drafting agents and a cited conversational interface will rarely hold eight cards at full draw. It uses the national average price because the paper names no state; a fab's own negotiated tariff will differ. The reseller price is before sales tax, freight and installation, and a written quote will differ.

Why this hardware: the paper's sizing line is explicit, "753 billion parameters served at FP8 need a full node of the 141 GB HBM GPU class, eight GPUs per node" (chapter 3, section 3.1), Table 4 fixes the class as "141 GB HBM GPU class, 8 GPUs per node, on the operator's own hardware inside the fab", and Figure 9 records that the sizing table "fixed the GLM 5.3 node count at one". Eight H200 cards at 141 GB are 1,128 GB, and that is the node priced, as Thinkmate's HGX H200 configuration and as p5en.48xlarge, whose eight H200 cards carry the same 1,128 GB (AWS 2026c).

One inconsistency in the paper's own sizing, which does not change the node count or the price: chapter 3 and Figure 9 fix one node, while chapter 7, section 7.1, chapter 8, section 8.1 and Table 4 say the footprint is unsized and no GPU count is derived until a verified model row stands. This appendix prices the one node; if the verified row changes the footprint, the node count and every line above scale with it.

### A.3 What the Price Does Not Include

- **The edge estate.** One octa core 6 TOPS NPU SoC unit per inspection tool group, in a fanless sealed cleanroom enclosure (Table 2; Table 4). The paper gives no unit price and no count of tool groups for the etch module.
- **Export control, which is a checkpoint, not a price.** The node is bought and run inside the United States, so no export license is priced for it. The control the paper does name binds people: access to fab technology by a supporting engineer who is a non-US person can be a deemed export under 15 CFR 734.13, so every supporting engineer is screened before access is granted (chapter 3, section 3.4; Table 5). That screening is a named approval and carries no line here.
- **Everything the paper's scope boundary keeps out**: new cameras, writes to tool control systems, ERP or supply chain integration, AMHS or robotics control and historic data migration (Table 2, "Out of scope").
- **The servers for the rest of the stack**: the Apache Kafka backbone, the object model store, InfluxDB 3 Core, K3s, the observability stack, Keycloak and the air gapped Harbor registry are chosen by product but not sized in the paper (chapter 4; Table 7).
- **People**: the engineers who build and run the platform, and the defect review engineers, yield engineers and process owners who confirm and approve every draft, whom every option carries.
- **Sales tax, freight and installation** on the hardware, which a written quote settles, and residual value at the end of three years.
- **Double counted cover.** The configured price already carries a three year depot warranty, so the support line may count some cover twice.
- **A closed model token comparison**, which is not printed because the paper states no token volume for the work surface.

ABSTRACT

## A Near Miss Should Be Data, Not Paper

The operation needs one question answered continuously across its four sites in the United States: where every trailer, slot, task and person is right now, and what should change next, from the door a carrier should back into, to the slot a fast-moving SKU should occupy and the walking a move would save, to the forklift and pedestrian near misses that occurred on today's shift and never reached anyone. No system the operation runs can answer it. The warehouse management system holds locations, inventory and pick paths but not labor, carriers or video; the labor system holds hours and rates but not the floor; the yard lives in a spreadsheet that is stale by mid-shift; roughly 220 cameras record for security and no one reviews them; and near misses are captured on paper, if at all. The documented cost of the failure is severe, because forklift and pedestrian incidents in warehousing are frequent and often serious or fatal (Cisco-eagle n.d.; OSHA 2023).

The design builds a live digital twin of each site as a system of context: an ontology of fourteen objects projected over five source systems through one adapter family, kept true by nightly reconciliation against the warehouse management system, which remains the system of record. Six services run on that model, from the live building twin, slotting intelligence and dock and yard scheduling to edge safety vision, platform and sovereignty, and the site manager assistant, and they reach people through four surfaces: a floor console for safety alarms, a clip review and coaching queue, the assistant work surface, and safety analytics. Safety vision processes the existing camera estate at each site on an industrial edge server with one 48 GB inference card, so only events and short clips leave the building, and no face recognition or re-identification runs anywhere. Five open-weight models carry the work: RF-DETR detection and OC-SORT tracking on the site edge GPU, a 27B dense model for assistant continuity when the wide area link drops, an embedding model for retrieval over records and procedures, and a 675B frontier assistant on one node of the company's own hardware, all under Apache-2.0 or MIT terms the operator holds outright.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure between existing systems, the constraints that fix where everything runs, the layered stack, the fourteen-object model and its typed links, ingestion through the adapter tier, the placement of inference across the edge, the site and the center, the five models and their licenses, the two-phase rollout with its item counts and exit gates, ownership of what the system builds, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

PART I · CHAPTER 1

## A Forklift Near Miss Never Becomes Data

Forklift and pedestrian incidents in warehousing are frequent, documented and often serious, yet the operation learns about them from paper after the fact, because no system it runs holds the building together.

The abstract promised a live digital twin of four buildings, built from data the operation already holds, with safety vision on cameras that already exist. This chapter states the question that twin exists to answer, what the absence of an answer costs when forklifts and pedestrians share a floor, and the scenario the design must fit without replacing anything.

### 1.1  The Question, the Data and the Rules

The question the operation needs answered is a daily one: where in each building is work unsafe or inefficient right now, and what single change this week would improve it. Answering it requires data no one system holds: the locations, inventory, open orders and pick paths of the warehouse management system; the shifts, zones and hours of the labor system; the trailers, carriers and appointments of the yard; and the continuous visual record of the cameras over docks, aisles and yards. It must satisfy the powered industrial truck standard, OSHA 1910.178, which governs forklift operation and operator evaluation, and the operator's own rule that associates' privacy is respected with no face recognition anywhere in the system. The ask also names open weights in the company's own environment, which places the regulatory ground alongside a sovereignty commitment.

### 1.2  The Documented Cost

The cost of the problem is documented and severe. Pedestrians suffer 26 percent of all forklift related injuries, and these injuries are often serious or fatal (Cisco-eagle n.d.). The fatality record shows the pattern repeating across jurisdictions: a lumber mill employee in Oregon died after being struck by a forklift (OHSU 2023); a major freight distribution company appeared in court after a forklift incident left a man fatally injured (GOVT 2018); and a potato producer was fined 180,000 dollars after a worker was seriously injured by a reversing forklift (SA 2025). The United States safety regulator has responded with a Regional Emphasis Program for powered industrial vehicles and warehousing operations, which raises inspection attention on exactly this hazard class (OSHA 2023). Each of these events was discovered after the fact. None of them became data at the moment they happened, which is the failure this design addresses.

### 1.3  The Operation as a Scenario

The scenario is a warehousing and intralogistics operator in the United States running four distribution centers. Each building has dock doors, racked storage aisles, a yard for trailers, and a shift-based workforce of associates, shift leads and a site manager; a supervisor reviews safety matters and a safety lead owns the program. About 220 fixed cameras across the estate already cover the docks, aisles and yards for security and record to a video management system. The operation runs five named systems: a warehouse management system, a labor management system, a yard management spreadsheet, the video management system and a carrier appointment source. The physical environments are the dock edge, where trailers meet doors and people; the aisle ends, where forklifts and pedestrians cross; and the yard, where trailers dwell and hostlers move. The regulatory ground is the powered industrial truck standard, state labor rules, and the operator's stated privacy rule. Four places, five systems, one building per site that no system holds whole.

PART I · CHAPTER 2

## Every System Sees One Slice of the Building

The warehouse management system, the labor system, the yard spreadsheet and the video estate each hold one true slice of the operation, and none of them can answer the questions that cross the slices.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the cost of leaving it unanswered. This chapter shows why no system the operator already runs can answer it: each holds one true slice of the building, and the questions that matter cross the slices.

### 2.1  What Each System Sees

The warehouse management system is the truth source for the building: locations, inventory, open orders, pick tasks and dock doors. What it misses is the physical world those records describe: it does not know who is standing at the aisle end, how fast a truck took the corner, or whether the exit the pick path relies on is blocked. The labor management system sees shifts, headcount by zone, hours and units per hour. It misses where the work physically happened and every hazard on the floor, because it records labor as numbers, not as movement. The yard management spreadsheet sees trailers, carriers and yard slots as they were last typed. It misses live dwell time, door state and arrival reality, and it depends on someone remembering to update it. The video management system sees everything: every dock, aisle and yard, recorded continuously. It misses meaning, because a recording is not a detection, an event or an alert, and no camera view is linked to an order, a shift or a slot. The carrier appointment source sees booked appointments and carriers. It misses arrival actuals, unload progress and which door a trailer should take. Figure 2 sets these five systems side by side, each sees column honest and each misses column decisive.

![Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.](figures/figure_02.png)

Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

### 2.2  What None of Them See Together

The questions that matter need all five slices at once, and no join exists. Which slotting move saves the most walking needs pick tasks, slot locations and SKU velocity together with labor by zone. Which door a trailer should take needs appointments, live unload rates and labor on shift. Whether an aisle end is dangerous needs the camera view, the shift schedule and the pick path that sends people through it. Today those answers are assembled by people, from a spreadsheet, a screen and a walk down the floor, which is why a near miss at an aisle crossing produces a paper report weeks later or nothing at all. The cost in practice is threefold: safety learning arrives after the fact, slotting decisions run on stale velocity, and carrier wait time is invisible until a carrier complains. The design's object model is the join these systems never had.

PART II · CHAPTER 3

## Four Rules Fix Where Everything Runs

Video processed at each site, no face recognition, safety functions left with certified equipment, and open weights in the company's own environment: these four rules settle the placement of every component downstream.

Chapter 2 showed that the join failure is structural: five systems, five slices, no shared model. The design could repair that join in many shapes, and four rules from the operator's own requirement settle which shape survives: where video runs, what vision may never do, who keeps the safety function, and whose environment the weights live in.

### 3.1  Video Is Processed at Each Site

The first rule is that video is processed at each site, and only events and short clips leave the building. This is hard in warehousing because the camera estate is large, about 220 fixed cameras, and the tempting architecture is a cloud analytics service that ingests every stream. That path is closed twice over: it moves raw video across the wide area link, and it puts the detection weights in someone else's environment. The rule forces inference onto an edge server at each distribution center, sized from the measured decode and inference budget on the camera substreams, with the one-way egress path made a physical property rather than a configuration promise.

### 3.2  No Face Recognition, No Re-identification

The second rule is that associates' privacy is respected and no face recognition runs anywhere. This is hard because safety vision watches people by design, and the easiest way to make tracking robust is a re-identification branch that learns what a person looks like. The design holds the line structurally: the tracker is motion-only, with no appearance model, so a detection is a moving object in a zone and never a named individual. The payoff is adoption as much as compliance, because a safety system the floor reads as surveillance stops being told anything.

### 3.3  Analytics Advise, Certified Equipment Stops

The third rule is that camera analytics are an operational feedback loop, never a safety-rated stop. The powered industrial truck standard already assigns safety functions to certified equipment and trained operators, and nothing in this design takes one over: no autonomous control of forklifts, doors or any equipment. This is hard because the vision system will sometimes see a hazard a person misses, and the urge to act directly is strong. The design answers with people deciding coaching: every safety event becomes a clip a supervisor reviews, and the machine's job is to capture the near miss that paper never caught.

### 3.4  Open Weights in the Company's Own Environment

The fourth rule is that data and models stay in the company's own environment, on open weights. This is hard at the scale the assistant needs: the frontier-class work surface model carries hundreds of billions of parameters, and hosting it in-country on operator hardware rules out the hosted API that would otherwise be the simple answer. Every model in the stack therefore carries a license the operator can hold outright, with no revenue trigger and no attribution duty, from the edge detection checkpoints to the site-tier assistant model that keeps each building answering when the wide area link drops.

### 3.5  Scoping Decisions and Their Costs

Three scoping decisions follow from the rules, each buying something specific at a stated cost, and Table 1 records them. They keep the warehouse management system as the system of record, replace only the yard spreadsheet, and place video processing at each site rather than centrally.

Table 1 · Scoping Decisions

| Decision | What it buys | What it costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Process video on edge servers at each site | Only events and short clips leave the building, as a physical property of the egress path | An industrial edge server with an inference GPU at each of the four sites, owned and supported by the operator |
| Keep the WMS as the system of record | The twin never argues with the source of inventory and orders; truth is maintained by reconciliation | The twin is only as live as the WMS event surface, which phase one measures before any dependent capability ships |
| Replace only the yard management spreadsheet | Dock and yard scheduling gains a system of record, and carrier wait time becomes visible | The new module must hold every field the spreadsheet held before the spreadsheet can retire |

### 3.6  What the Design Chose Against

The rules also settle the rejected alternatives, and Table 2 records where each choice was made and what it turned down. The final row states the scope boundary: what the design deliberately does not do, and why each exclusion protects a rule stated above.

Table 2 · What the Design Chose Against

| Where | What was picked | Instead of, and why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety vision | An open source pipeline on site edge servers, with RF-DETR detection and OC-SORT tracking under zone rules | A packaged camera-analytics service or analytics built into the video management system, because only events and clips may leave the building and open weights on the operator's own servers are owned outright |
| The site manager assistant | Frontier open weights self-hosted on operator hardware under Apache-2.0 | A hosted frontier model API, because data and models must stay in the company's own environment |
| Speeding detection | Ground-plane calibrated speeds in meters per second from fixed cameras | Pixel-space speed heuristics, because a speeding call in a pedestrian zone must survive a challenge, and only a calibrated pixel-to-ground mapping is a measured speed |
| The camera estate | Reuse the existing cameras through a six-gate survey, with purpose-placed fixed additions only where a view fails | A new camera estate, because the ask is to run on the existing cameras and the survey turns reuse into recorded evidence |
| Positioning of people and vehicles | Positions from the calibrated camera views the safety vision already needs | Wearable or vehicle tags, because tagging people would change the privacy posture without adding a detection the cameras cannot already make |
| Scope boundary | Out of scope: no face recognition or re-identification, no autonomous control of equipment, no WMS replacement, no production fine-tuning of weights | Each included alternative would break a stated rule: a re-identification branch turns safety into surveillance, an automated stop is a safety-rated function, the WMS stays the system of record, and the system improves through memory rather than weight changes |

PART II · CHAPTER 4

## One Stack Reaches From Records to the Floor

A layered stack runs from the five systems of record, through one adapter family and an ontology of fourteen objects, up to six services and four surfaces the site teams actually use.

Chapter 3 settled the constraints: the systems of record stay, data stays inside the company's environment, people decide every action, and a pilot gate can stop the work cheaply. This chapter lays out the stack those constraints produce, layer by layer, from the systems of record to the surfaces the floor teams touch.

### 4.1  A Three-Tier Pattern and Why It Fits

The pattern is three tiers. Below sit the five systems of record: the warehouse management system, the labor management system, the yard management spreadsheet, the video management system and the carrier appointment source. In the middle sits one object model, held in an ontology store on the operator's own hardware, that projects those records as fourteen objects with typed links and stays true by reconciling against them rather than by becoming a record itself. Above sit the applications and agents: six services that reason over the twin and four surfaces that people actually use. Nothing above the middle tier writes a source system, and nothing below the middle tier is replaced except the yard spreadsheet, which the dock and yard scheduling module retires.

This shape fits the operation for three reasons. The warehouse management system keeps its position as the system of record, so the twin never competes with it for truth. Safety vision runs at each site on the existing camera estate of roughly 220 fixed IP cameras, so video is processed in the building and only events and short clips ever leave it. And the same ontology serves slotting, dock and yard scheduling, safety and the site manager assistant, so each capability strengthens the others instead of building its own data island. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with the count at each layer: five sources, one adapter family, fourteen objects, six services and four surfaces.

![Figure 3. The layered stack: 5 sources, 1 adapter family, 14 objects, 6 services and 4 surfaces.](figures/figure_03.png)

Figure 3. The layered stack: 5 sources, 1 adapter family, 14 objects, 6 services and 4 surfaces.

### 4.2  The Stack Stage by Stage

Table 3 walks the stack stage by stage, and each stage names its components so an engineer can trace any capability to the software that carries it. Two stages deserve comment. Sensing is deliberately reuse-heavy: the existing camera estate already covers the docks, aisles and yards, so the design adds only purpose-placed fixed cameras where the six-gate reuse survey fails a view. Inference is split by latency and privacy: vision runs in Triton Inference Server on a 48 GB PCIe inference GPU class card in each site's industrial edge server, the site-tier language model runs under vLLM on the same card so the assistant survives a wide area link loss, and the frontier model that carries the assistant work surface runs on one node of the 141 GB HBM class centrally.

The remaining stages carry the operation of the stack itself: k3s orchestrates containers on the edge servers, Harbor holds the air-gapped artifact and model registry, CVAT supports clip labeling for accuracy measurement, and Prometheus, Grafana and Loki observe the running system, so a stalled adapter or a hot GPU is visible the same day.

Table 3 · The Stack, Stage by Stage

| Stage | What it is responsible for | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sources | Being right: locations, inventory, open orders, labor, appointments and video | Five named systems: the warehouse management system, the labor management system, the yard management spreadsheet, the video management system and the carrier appointment source |
| Sensing | Turning the physical site into signals | The existing estate of roughly 220 fixed IP cameras, the WMS event stream, labor management extracts, the yard appointment feed, wide area link and GPU health telemetry, all timed from a GNSS-disciplined PTP grandmaster |
| Adapters | Bringing every source through one gate, provenance stamped | One integration adapter family: Debezium change data capture against the transactional systems, MediaMTX for camera streams, normalized events onto the backbone |
| Object model | Holding the fourteen objects and their typed links | an ontology store, kept true by nightly reconciliation against the sources, with telemetry in InfluxDB 3 Core |
| Inference | Running the five models where latency and privacy demand | Triton Inference Server on the 48 GB edge GPU class per site for vision, vLLM on the same card for the site-tier Qwen3.8-27B, one 141 GB HBM class node for the frontier Mistral Large 3 675B |
| Services | Delivering the six capabilities | Live building twin, slotting intelligence, dock and yard scheduling, edge safety vision, platform and sovereignty, and the site manager assistant |
| Surfaces | What people touch | Four surfaces: the live floor console on a tablet, the clip review and coaching queue, the assistant work surface over the twin, and safety analytics |

PART II · CHAPTER 5

## Fourteen Objects Turn Site Data Into One Argument

Fourteen objects and their typed links let one query walk from a trailer at a dock door to the pick task, associate and shift it will touch, a join no document store can make.

Chapter 4 fixed the layers and their counts. This chapter opens the middle layer: the fourteen objects, the typed links between them, and the guarantees that make the model safe for a person to act on.

### 5.1  Fourteen Objects and Their Typed Links

Fourteen objects carry the whole twin. Distribution Center is anchored in the WMS site master and holds each building's square footage, dock door count, shift pattern, camera count and WAN link. Dock Door and Yard Trailer are anchored in the yard management spreadsheet until the new dock and yard module takes over as the yard system of record. Storage Slot, SKU, Open Order and Pick Task are anchored in the WMS. Associate and Labor Shift are anchored in the labor management system. Camera Zone is anchored in the video management system. Safety Event digitizes what paper near-miss reports hold today. Forklift, Shift Lead and Slotting Recommendation are native to the design.

The typed links are what make this an argument rather than an archive, and Figure 4 draws all of them. A query can start at a Yard Trailer, walk to the Dock Door it is staged at, on to the SKUs whose travel distance from dock is measured, to the Pick Tasks those SKUs feed, to the Associate each task is assigned to, and finish at the Shift Lead who owns that associate's shift: one traversal from a trailer in the yard to the labor it will consume and the person accountable for it. A document store holds each of those records as a separate document, so the same question needs a hand-written join at every hop, and the slotting service, the dock scheduler and the assistant each rebuild the same joins privately. Here the joins are declared once, and every service reads the same ones.

![Figure 4. The fourteen objects of the model and the typed links that let a query reach across them.](figures/figure_04.png)

Figure 4. The fourteen objects of the model and the typed links that let a query reach across them.

### 5.2  The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the status vocabularies. A Slotting Recommendation moves through Drafted, Approved, Executed, Realized or Expired, and it states predicted walking saved and move labor estimate before anyone approves it. A Safety Event moves from Detected through Under review and Confirmed to Coaching scheduled, Closed or Dismissed as false, with a supervisor deciding coaching every time. The hosting posture keeps that loop inside the company: every component runs in the operator's own environment, identity is Keycloak on site, there are no external service links, and the five models are open weights served locally, with only events and short clips leaving a building through a hardware-enforced one-way egress. The ontology's only write path is the adapter tier, so no service writes the twin directly; approved slotting moves execute in the WMS, and the WMS remains the system of record.

### 5.3  One Object in Its Recorded Form

The Distribution Center object shows how the design records each site, in the exact form the ontology stores it.

```
{ "id": "distribution-center", "label": "Distribution Center", "kind": "site", "anchored_in": "The WMS site master", "properties": [ "Square footage", "Dock door count", "Shift pattern", "Camera count", "WAN link" ], "status_vocabulary": [], "links": [ { "to": "dock-door", "label": "has" }, { "to": "shift-lead", "label": "runs" }, { "to": "camera-zone", "label": "covers" } ] }
```

PART II · CHAPTER 6

## Five Systems Feed the Twin Through One Gate

Every source enters through the adapter tier, never directly, so the twin's picture can be reconciled against the systems of record it projects and drift is caught the same day.

Chapter 5 showed what the object model holds. This chapter covers how data reaches it: five named sources, one adapter family, and an event backbone that keeps order even when the wide area link does not.

### 6.1  Five Sources and Their Provenance

Figure 5 maps the five sources and their provenance classes. Four are confirmed at intake as the operator's own systems, all read-only to the design: the warehouse management system, the twin's truth source for locations, inventory, open orders and pick tasks; the labor management system, feeding associates and labor shifts as well as the live unload rates dock scheduling leans on; the yard management spreadsheet, imported once and then retired as the dock and yard module becomes the yard system of record; and the video management system, whose roughly 220 recorded cameras the safety vision rides rather than replaces. The fifth, the carrier appointment source, is domain-typical: the requirement names appointments but not the system behind them, so a class-typical booking feed enters through the same adapter with its provenance marked, and every downstream consumer can see which facts rest on an assumed source until the operator names the real one.

![Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.](figures/figure_05.png)

Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

### 6.2  What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One adapter family, the integration adapter, stands between every source and the ontology, and it guarantees four things. Every object carries provenance: the source system, the timestamp and the offset it came from, so any figure on any surface traces back to its record. Every write is an idempotent upsert keyed on the natural identifier, so a replayed stream cannot duplicate a trailer or a pick task. Every unit and coordinate is normalized on the way in: aisle, bay and level for slots, meters per second for calibrated speeds. And every night the adapter tier counts objects against the systems of record and surfaces drift the same day, which is what keeps a projection honest. The warehouse management system stays read-only throughout; the only system the design replaces is the yard spreadsheet.

### 6.3  The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.3, in KRaft mode, is the backbone. Ordering is per key: events for one dock door, one SKU or one camera zone land on one partition and keep their order, and linuxptp with chrony keeps camera clocks and server clocks close enough that a forklift event and a WMS event order correctly against each other. Delivery is at-least-once into idempotent consumers, so nothing is lost to a restart. Buffering is sized for the survival window at the measured event and clip rate, then doubled, so a wide area outage longer than expected drops nothing: events and clips accumulate on site storage and flow when the link returns. Replication covers the central aggregation across the four sites, Harbor carries the air-gapped artifact and model registry, InfluxDB 3 Core holds telemetry, and Prometheus, Grafana and Loki observe the whole path, so the backbone's own health is as visible as the site's.

PART II · CHAPTER 7

## Detection Belongs at the Edge and Reasoning in House

Detection and tracking run on a site edge server so only events and short clips leave the building, the site keeps a degraded-mode assistant on its own card, and the frontier weights run on the company's own central hardware.

Chapter 6 described how five source systems enter through adapters and land in the object model as events. This chapter decides where the intelligence that reads those events runs: which models sit beside the cameras, which sit beside the associates, and which sit on the company's own central hardware.

### 7.1  Three Tiers, Each with a Reason

The design places inference at three tiers, and Figure 6 shows all of them together: the edge tier on each site's rack server, the site tier on the same box, and the central tier in the operator's own environment. The edge tier carries the vision stack: RF-DETR detection checkpoints watching forklifts, order pickers, pedestrians, vests, pallets and trailers on the camera substreams, OC-SORT associating detections into tracks so one event becomes one alert rather than ten, and the zone rules that turn a track into a proximity, speeding or blocked-exit event. Detection belongs here because the constraint is explicit: video is processed at each site, and only events and short clips leave the building. The site tier carries Qwen3.8-27B, whose FP8 weights are about 31 GB and fit one 48 GB PCIe inference card with headroom for its KV cache, so the site manager assistant keeps answering when the wide area link drops, alongside BGE-M3 for embedding retrieval over safety records and procedures at about 1.1 GB in FP16. The central tier carries Mistral Large 3 675B, the frontier work surface model, on one node of the 141 GB HBM class: eight cards give about 1,038 GB of usable memory at 0.92 utilization, the FP8 weights published at about 682 GB fit inside it, and roughly 350 GB of KV ceiling remains for concurrent assistant sessions across the estate. The arithmetic is the argument: each tier's weights, usable memory and KV ceiling were checked before anything else about the tier was decided, because a model that does not fit is not a placement choice.

![Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.](figures/figure_06.png)

Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

### 7.2  The Latency Budget

The budget follows the two-clocks rule the design set in its first principles: milliseconds on the truck, seconds in orchestration. The safety path is the tight one. A pedestrian stepping into an aisle end must be detected, tracked and raised as an alarm to the shift lead's live floor console within the time a person can still act, which is why detection and tracking run on the edge GPU next to the cameras rather than round a wide area link. Temporal confirmation on event tubes trades a small amount of that time for precision, because an alarm the floor learns to ignore is worse than no alarm at all; the alert budget is set before thresholds, and per-camera dismissal trends are watched weekly. The assistant path runs on the seconds clock: a site manager asks the twin a question, retrieval over the ontology and BGE-M3 embeddings assembles the context, and the model answers in conversational time. Slotting intelligence has no latency pressure at all and runs weekly against reconciled data, which is why it reads the twin rather than the raw streams.

### 7.3  What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails

Only two things cross the site boundary: safety events with short clips, and the telemetry and twin aggregates the central tier reads. The events-and-clips path can be hardened with a hardware-enforced one-way egress option, which makes "only events and short clips leave the building" a physical property rather than a configuration promise; lidi and Eurydice are the verified transfer software beside the diode. When the wide area link fails, the site does not stop: detection, tracking, the live floor console and the degraded-mode assistant on the 27B card all continue locally, and a store-and-forward buffer sized for the survival window at the measured event and clip rate, then doubled, holds everything until the link returns; the longest historical outage at each site is a discovery question, not an assumption. When power fails, the edge node and its PoE switches ride one UPS, and Network UPS Tools v2.8.5 orders a clean shutdown before the battery runs out, so the object model resynchronizes rather than corrupts. When the update path is the failure, each site pulls container images and model weights from a Harbor registry inside the operator's own environment, so an update that cannot reach a site leaves that site running its last good versions rather than reaching for the internet. No failure in the link, the power or the update path puts a camera stream outside the building.

PART II · CHAPTER 8

## The Licenses Decide What the Operator Owns

Each of the five models carries a license the operator can live inside, and the terms of those licenses, with their triggers and attribution duties, drove the picks rather than convenience.

Chapter 7 placed each model at its tier and checked the memory arithmetic. This chapter examines the licenses those models carry, because the requirement that data and models stay in the company's own environment on open weights makes the license terms, not the benchmark scores, the deciding factor. Figure 7 sets the five models out as one stack. The frontier tier is Mistral Large 3 675B, a 675 billion parameter instruct model serving the agentic work surface and ontology maintenance: the site manager assistant over the twin, and the surface the operator's own people build agents on. Its published FP8 checkpoint is about 682 GB, which its publisher states fits one node of eight 141 GB HBM class GPUs or 192 GB HBM class GPUs, while the NVFP4 build fits a node of 80 GB class cards. It runs centrally on the operator's own hardware, and it is Apache-2.0: no revenue trigger, no attribution duty, so the operator owns the weights outright. It was chosen over GLM 5.3, whose publisher is on the US Entity List, and over Mistral-licensed neighbors whose revenue triggers would engage as the estate grows. The site tier is Qwen3.8-27B, a dense Apache-2.0 model whose footprint is about 56 GB at 16 bit, about 28 GB at 8 bit and about 14 GB at 4 bit, weights only, which is why one 48 GB PCIe card holds it at FP8 with KV headroom for assistant continuity during WAN loss. It was picked from the small-on-site family for one-card density and long context. The embedding model is BGE-M3, MIT licensed with an 8,192 token window, so a whole standard operating procedure stays one passage; it produces dense, sparse and multi-vector output from one pass, which keeps error codes and slot identifiers retrievable on a small box, and it occupies about 1.1 GB at FP16 from a published 2.27 GB at float32. The vision tier is RF-DETR for detection: the rfdetr package and its Nano to Large detection checkpoints are Apache-2.0, occupying about 61 to 68 MB at 16 bit, and take site fine-tuning for evaluation sets; the XL and 2XL checkpoints in rfdetr\_plus carry a platform license, so the design uses N through L only. It was chosen over D-FINE for the segmentation path and over YOLO26, whose AGPL gate is wrong for a system the operator owns. Beside it runs OC-SORT for multi-object tracking: MIT licensed, motion-only, built for objects that turn and stop unpredictably, which forklifts and pedestrians at aisle ends are, with association running at about 700 FPS on a CPU given detections. It has no re-identification branch, which keeps the privacy posture the constraint sets, and it was picked over the Roboflow trackers collection for license minimalism on the hot path. Together these choices answer the regulatory ground beneath them: the safety vision exists because pedestrians suffer 26 percent of all forklift related injuries, often serious or fatal (Cisco-eagle n.d.), and the US safety regulator's regional emphasis program on powered industrial vehicles and warehousing operations shows where enforcement attention sits (OSHA 2023).

Figure 7. The five models, their placement, and the work each one does.
